Positional encoding schemes must assign each token a representation of where it sits in a sequence, and models trained on sequences up to length N develop strong inductive biases around those positions — the central question is whether those representations generalize smoothly when inference-time sequences exceed N, or whether they degrade catastrophically. The key concepts are: (1) the geometry of position space (absolute vs. relative vs. rotary encodings and how each interpolates or extrapolates), (2) attention score magnitude as a function of positional distance, and (3) the distribution shift between seen and unseen position indices. A beginner assumes that RoPE or ALiBi "solves" extrapolation because they're relative and theoretically unbounded — the expert knows that theoretical unboundedness and empirical stability are entirely different things: attention entropy collapses, specific heads lose their ability to distinguish positions at long range, and perplexity often spikes sharply at a threshold well below 2×N. The subtler failure that non-experts miss is that degradation is rarely uniform — models often maintain fluency on local coherence tasks while silently failing at long-range dependencies, so standard perplexity metrics mask the problem entirely. This means a model can appear to handle long contexts while retrieving nothing useful from tokens beyond its training horizon.

Failure manifests at the dot-product attention score computation — specifically when the query and key vectors, each rotated by their respective RoPE angles θ·m and θ·n, produce inner products whose magnitude and relative ordering become unreliable for position indices m or n unseen during training. RoPE applies rotation matrices at each attention head before the QK dot product, so the pathology is localized there: for high-frequency dimensions (large θ_d), the rotation completes full cycles at short distances and stays stable, but for low-frequency dimensions (small θ_d), the rotation at extrapolated positions lands in angular territory the model never optimized against, producing attention logits that are out-of-distribution in a structured, dimension-specific way. The Su et al. RoPE paper shows that the expected inner product decays with relative distance, but this decay profile is only calibrated for distances seen in training — beyond that boundary, some dimensions oscillate into destructive interference rather than graceful decay. This precise localization is why position interpolation (Chen et al., 2023, "Extending Context Window of Large Language Models via Positional Interpolation") works: instead of extrapolating to unseen angles, it rescales all position indices by a factor of L_train/L_target, compressing new positions back into the trained angular range, requiring only ~1000 fine-tuning steps to restabilize attention patterns. The location also explains why interpolation beats naive extrapolation but still needs fine-tuning — the compression changes the relative angular gaps between nearby tokens, which disrupts short-range attention patterns that were previously well-calibrated, essentially robbing Peter to pay Paul across the frequency spectrum.

The asymmetry is fundamental: high-frequency RoPE dimensions (large base-angle θ_d) already cycle through full rotations within just a few tokens, so compressing their position scale does almost nothing harmful — those dimensions were never the ones failing at extrapolation anyway. Low-frequency dimensions (small θ_d) are the actual extrapolation problem, because they evolve slowly and carry long-range positional signal, but uniform interpolation compresses all dimensions equally, needlessly distorting the short-range signal in high-frequency dimensions to fix a problem that only lives in low-frequency ones. YaRN (Peng et al., 2023) exploits this directly by partitioning RoPE dimensions into three regimes — high-frequency dimensions get no scaling (they're fine as-is), low-frequency dimensions get full interpolation scaling, and mid-frequency dimensions get a blended "ramp" factor — allowing the fix to be targeted rather than uniform. In practice YaRN achieves competitive perplexity at 64k–128k context on LLaMA-2 with less fine-tuning degradation than uniform interpolation, precisely because it stops penalizing the dimensions that didn't need rescaling. The deeper implication is that "position interpolation" was always an approximation masking a dimension-heterogeneous problem, and any scheme that treats the RoPE frequency spectrum as a monolith is leaving quality on the table. This also suggests that the optimal interpolation strategy is model- and dataset-dependent, since the boundary between "safe" and "unsafe" frequency bands shifts with base frequency, head dimension, and the distance statistics of the training corpus.

The specific mechanism is that the QK projection weights were trained to expect inner products in a particular magnitude range for their learned queries and keys; rescaling positions changes the angular gaps and therefore the dot-product magnitudes systematically, and the softmax temperature (implicitly set by the scale factor 1/√d_k) is now miscalibrated relative to the new logit distribution. Empirically, "lost in the middle" behavior (Liu et al., 2023) is partly a symptom of this: models without proper long-context fine-tuning attend strongly to recency and primacy positions — which remain in-distribution — and systematically underweight middle-context tokens whose positional representations are most distorted. The heads most responsible for residual failure are identifiable by two signatures: (1) heads with high positional attention entropy variance across layers — heads that normally show sharp, distance-sensitive patterns but flatten at long range — and (2) heads in middle-to-late layers that handle long-range syntactic or coreference dependencies, as opposed to early layers doing local n-gram pattern matching which are relatively robust. Work on attention head probing (e.g., Clark et al. on BERT, extended in later decoder analyses) shows that a small subset of heads — sometimes fewer than 10% — carry the majority of long-range retrieval signal, meaning the extrapolation failure is concentrated rather than diffuse, and targeted interventions on those heads could in principle be more efficient than global fine-tuning.

The surgical fine-tuning intuition is appealing but breaks against a hard architectural fact: attention heads do not own information, the residual stream does. Each head reads from and writes back to a shared residual stream via low-rank projections (W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O), meaning a "long-range retrieval head" is consuming representations that were shaped by every earlier layer's attention and MLP operations — if those upstream components weren't fine-tuned for longer contexts, the queries and keys the targeted head receives are already corrupted relative to what fine-tuning would have produced. This is the core finding in LongLoRA (Chen et al., 2023): rather than targeting specific heads, they find that fine-tuning only the attention layers (not MLPs) with shift-short-attention during training is sufficient, but crucially this works because it lets all attention layers adapt their residual stream interactions jointly, not because any single head was the bottleneck. The residual stream decomposition also reveals a subtler problem: MLP layers function as key-value memories (Geva et al., 2021) that store factual associations indexed partly by position-dependent context; at extended lengths, the activated MLP "memories" may be systematically wrong because the residual stream representation arriving at each MLP has no long-context analog in training, making MLP outputs a second independent failure mode that surgical attention fine-tuning cannot address. Empirically this manifests as models that retrieve the existence of a long-range referent (attention partially fixed) but hallucinate its attributes (MLP lookup misfires), a dissociation that is hard to detect with standard needle-in-haystack benchmarks which only test retrieval presence. The conclusion is that context extension fine-tuning needs to be at minimum attention-layer-wide, and ideally includes MLP layers too — the apparent concentration of failure in specific heads was a diagnostic observation about where position encoding stress shows up first, not a prescription for where intervention is sufficient.

Facts encoded early in pretraining are represented in MLP weight space through highly redundant, distributed keys — they've been reinforced across many gradient steps and diverse contexts, making their retrieval relatively robust to positional distribution shift because the key vectors that activate them are broad and overlapping. Late-learned facts, by contrast, have sparse, narrow key representations (fewer reinforcing examples, less weight consolidation), meaning their MLP lookup is more sensitive to the exact residual stream state arriving at that layer — and at extended context lengths, that residual stream carries positional contamination that pushes activation patterns away from the narrow basin needed to retrieve the sparse fact correctly. This predicts a specific vulnerability pattern: documents containing information that was rare or late-appearing in the training corpus — recent events, niche technical details, less-common named entities — are most susceptible to attribute hallucination at long context, because their MLP keys have the least fault tolerance for off-distribution residual stream inputs. The "lost in the middle" phenomenon (Liu et al., 2023, showing accuracy drops from ~70% at context boundaries to ~40% in the middle for 20-document retrieval tasks) likely conflates two distinct failure modes: positional attention failure (the head doesn't route to the right token) and this MLP attribute failure (attention routes correctly but the subsequent MLP lookup retrieves the wrong attribute because the residual stream context is unfamiliar). Practically this means that stuffing a long context with documents about obscure or recent entities is disproportionately risky — the model may correctly identify which document is relevant (attention working) while confabulating specifics from more heavily-trained, semantically adjacent facts (MLP substituting a high-confidence nearby memory for the sparse correct one). This substitution pattern is particularly insidious because the hallucinated attributes are not random noise but plausible interpolations from well-trained neighboring facts, making them hard to detect without ground-truth verification.

Yes, the MLP key space neighborhood structure is a first-class determinant — this is precisely what the knowledge neurons line of work (Dai et al., 2022) and Geva et al.'s fact-tracing experiments demonstrate: specific MLP neurons in middle-to-late layers activate for semantically coherent clusters, and when a target fact's key is weakly represented, the model doesn't fail silently but instead activates the strongest neighboring key, producing a confident wrong answer that is semantically coherent with the cluster. The structure can be partially audited through causal tracing (Meng et al., ROME, 2022), which identifies which MLP layers and positions are causally responsible for a given factual output by patching activations and measuring output change — this gives you a map of where specific facts live and how isolated versus clustered their representations are, with isolated facts showing sharp single-layer causal responsibility and clustered facts showing diffuse multi-layer responsibility. A pre-deployment audit would involve: identifying facts in your target domain, running causal traces to measure their representation sharpness, then deliberately constructing adversarial long-context probes that place semantically neighboring facts in the same context to measure substitution rates — if neighbor B consistently contaminates retrieval of target A, you've found a deployment-relevant interference pair. The practical obstacle is scaling: ROME-style causal tracing requires O(L × T) forward passes per fact (L layers, T token positions), which is tractable for hundreds of facts but not millions, so full pre-deployment auditing requires either sampling-based approximations or restricting the audit to high-stakes entity clusters. Recent work on representation engineering (Zou et al., 2023) suggests a complementary angle — you can read out the "confidence geometry" of a representation directly from the residual stream without exhaustive causal tracing, potentially giving a cheaper signal for which facts are at substitution risk. The unsettling implication is that two models with identical benchmark accuracy can have radically different substitution vulnerability profiles depending on their pretraining data distribution, meaning standard evals are blind to this failure mode entirely.

In-context learning does not overwrite MLP memories — it competes via the residual stream through a mechanism that is now reasonably well characterized: attention heads in middle-to-late layers perform what Olsson et al. (2022) call "induction" and what subsequent work frames as context vs. memory arbitration, where the residual stream accumulates a superposition of the MLP's parametric prediction and the attention mechanism's in-context evidence, with the final output determined by which signal dominates at the last layer's unembedding projection. Crucially, causal tracing's assumption of static storage breaks because the residual stream arriving at a fact-storing MLP layer is now different — it carries in-context information that shifts the input away from the key vector the MLP was trained to respond to, effectively reducing the MLP's "vote" for its stored fact even before any competition at the output layer. This was demonstrated concretely by Hernandez et al. (2023) in their context vs. memory counterfactual experiments: when in-context evidence contradicts a parametric fact, the MLP layer responsible for that fact still activates and still pushes toward the stored answer, but attention-mediated context writes a competing vector into the residual stream that partially cancels it — the model follows context not because memory is suppressed but because the vector sum tips toward the contextual answer. The failure mode at long context is therefore a signal-to-noise degradation: at short context lengths the in-context evidence is written cleanly into the residual stream by well-calibrated attention; at long context lengths, positional encoding failure means the attention heads doing context retrieval are miscalibrated, so they write a weaker or noisier contextual vector, and the MLP parametric memory — which is unaffected by positional encoding — wins by default even when the context contains the correct answer. This explains a specific empirical pattern: models are more likely to ignore correct in-context information and revert to parametric answers as context length increases, not because they "forgot" the context but because the arbitration balance tips toward MLP memory when attention-mediated context writing degrades. The practical implication is severe — retrieval-augmented generation systems assume that providing correct context will override wrong parametric memory, but at long context lengths this assumption weakens precisely when RAG is being asked to do the most work.
